blocks.md: The Solow model is the simplest model of long-run growth. Output is made from technology, machines and workers. Technology and the number of workers are taken as given; the stock of machines is built up inside the model. People save a fixed share of their income, and those savings become new machines. Machines wear out, and each extra machine adds less output than the last. So an economy that keeps saving eventually reaches a point where new investment only just replaces what wears out — it stops getting richer from saving alone. An economy that starts with more machines than that runs down to the same point. Only better technology keeps living standards rising.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It separates what saving can do (make a country permanently richer in level) from what only innovation can do (keep it growing), and it predicts that economies far from their steady state change fastest.

Robert Solow's 1956 model of long-run growth: households save a constant fraction of income, saving becomes capital, and capital has diminishing returns. In the basic version technology $A$ and labor $L$ are constant, and capital per worker follows
converging to the steady state
Three sources of growth enter through Cobb-Douglas production, $Y = AK^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}$ ([Cobb-Douglas Production Function](note:cobb-douglas-production-function)):

| Source | Role | Status ([Endogenous and Exogenous Variables](note:endogenous-and-exogenous-variables)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $A$ — technology | Multiplies output | **Exogenous** |
| $K$ — capital | Accumulated from saving | **Endogenous** |
| $L$ — labor | Workers | **Exogenous** |

Behaviour: output is split into consumption and saving at a **fixed saving rate** $s$; saving equals investment ([Saving-Investment Identity](note:saving-investment-identity)) and generates new capital; capital depreciates at rate $\delta$ each period.

**Per worker.** Divide production by $L$: $Y/L = AK^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}/L = A(K/L)^{\alpha}$, so $y = Ak^{\alpha}$. Divide the law of motion by the (constant) $L$:
This step needs $L$ constant; with a growing workforce see [Solow Model with Technological Progress](note:solow-model-with-technological-progress).

blocks.title: Reading the formula
blocks.md: Numerator = what goes in ($sA$). Denominator = what leaks out ($\delta$). The exponent $1/(1-\alpha) > 1$ amplifies the ratio because more capital produces more output, which is partly saved again. With $\alpha = 1/3$ the exponent is 1.5, so doubling $s$ raises $\bar{k}$ by $2^{1.5} = 2.83\times$ — and $\bar{y}$ by only $2^{0.5} = 1.41\times$.
Graphically, the steady state is where the concave investment curve $sf(k)$ crosses the depreciation line $\delta k$ — see [Solow Diagram](note:solow-diagram).

blocks.md: Starting above the steady state, capital falls toward it — quickly at first, then more slowly as the gap between investment and depreciation shrinks:

The initial gap of 75 halves by period 12 ($k_{12} = 61.24$, a gap of 36.2). Near $\bar{k}$ the gap shrinks by a factor $1 - (1-\alpha)\delta = 0.95$ each period (see the stability example in [Steady State](note:steady-state)). Starting below $\bar{k}$ the mirror image happens: capital grows, fastest when furthest away. This is **conditional convergence** — toward each economy's own $\bar{k}$, which depends on $s$, $A$, $\delta$ and $\alpha$.
Parameter changes move $\bar{k}$; capital then travels there gradually and output $y = Ak^{\alpha}$ follows.

| Change | $\bar{k}$ | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Saving rate $s$ up | ↑ | $s$: 0.5 → 0.6 gives $\bar{k}$: 25 → 36 |
| Depreciation $\delta$ up | ↓ | $\delta$: 0.1 → 0.125 gives $\bar{k}$: 25 → 16 |
| Technology $A$ up | ↑ | — |
| One-off loss of capital | Unchanged | $k$ rebuilds to the old $\bar{k}$ |
The graphs for each case, with time paths, are in [Solow Diagram](note:solow-diagram).

Consumption per worker is $c = (1-s)y$. A rise in $s$ works through two channels: it cuts the share consumed **immediately**, and it raises $k$ and therefore $y$ **over time**. At the extremes consumption is zero: $s = 1$ gives high output but nothing consumed; $s = 0$ gives no capital and no output. In between, steady-state consumption peaks at the [Golden Rule Saving Rate](note:golden-rule-saving-rate), $s = \alpha$ under Cobb-Douglas.
In the example ($\alpha = 1/2$), $\bar{c} = 10s(1-s)$:
The example economy, with $s = 1/2 = \alpha$, is exactly at the golden rule.

With labor growing at $\eta$ and TFP at $\gamma$, capital per worker never settles. Dividing by effective labor restores a steady state, $\tilde{k} \to (s/(\delta+\eta+\tilde{\gamma}))^{1/(1-\alpha)}$ with $\tilde{\gamma} = \gamma/(1-\alpha)$, along which output per worker grows at $\tilde{\gamma}$ forever — the [Balanced Growth Path](note:balanced-growth-path). Saving still affects only levels; sustained growth in living standards needs technological progress. Details in [Solow Model with Technological Progress](note:solow-model-with-technological-progress).

- Saying higher saving raises the long-run *growth rate*. It raises the steady-state *level*; growth is faster only during the transition.
- Letting capital jump after a parameter change — it is a stock and moves only through the law of motion.
- Dividing by $L$ as if it were constant when the workforce grows.
- Thinking the aim is to maximize capital: the golden rule maximizes *consumption*.
- Macro: growth accounting, convergence across countries, development policy; the benchmark that optimal-saving (Ramsey) models are compared against.
